title: The Comedy About Spies is BACK! But do I still like it?
transcript: I went to go and see the comedy about spies, and I have to tell you exactly what I thought about it. Now, comedy about spies was my most watched show of 2025. So, how did it stack up seeing it in 2026? Given that it's in a brand new theater, and it's been altered in a couple of ways. I mean, I think the first thing I have to say is the fact that I absolutely adored it. I mean, it was a Mischief show, and I mean, as a Mischief show, it is very rare for a Mischief show not to appeal to me, and I'm very pleased to see this back on the West End, even if it is just for a limited run. Now, I must confess I have actually already seen this twice since I went to see it for the first time now that it's at the Adelphi Theatre. So, this review is coming after I've already seen it multiple times, but I feel that actually clue you in as to how this review is about to go. I absolutely adore this production, and I actually really, really love the changes they've made. The first thing I have to compliment is, of course, the cast. The Mischief performers are out of this world hilarious. Their chemistry, their understanding of their characters, the physicality, their comedic timing, everything is just spot-on. Of course, Chris Lees as Sergei is my favorite character in the comedy about spies. There is just something so charming and so endearing about him, but also ultimately something so funny about the way that he is prepared to kind of like flail himself about on stage to bring the character to life. And I think he played really well off of Bryony Corrigan's Elena. If you didn't know, Charlie Russell played Elena in the last production, and Bryony Corrigan is stepping in to play the role this time round, and it brings a beautiful new dynamic to the Elena-Sergei relationship, which I absolutely adored. I know a lot of people often criticize Mischief for always playing like the same characters. I myself have even said, "When you go and see a Mischief show without the original like Mischief members in it, you can often tell who which role was written for." But that isn't a criticism I can ever have when you are seeing these original members playing these roles because they do it so well. They've all got their comedy type that they execute so brilliantly that just makes them such a joy and such a treat to watch that you absolutely cannot fault them for. But cast aside, I think in talking about the highlights here, I'm going to mostly focus on the changes made. If you want to see my review of the original, go and find that somewhere. I don't know where I put it. But anyway, the most noticeable change for me was the set. In many places, this set has been plussed up, whilst the core elements of the original are still there. Now, this is a David Farley designed set, and I think he's done a fantastic job. But the main difference you will notice if you were familiar with last year's version of the production, is that we have several more pieces of set that will be lowered in at various points. So, what were moments that used to happen just in front of a curtain during the 2025 run, now have a piece of set behind them, which is usually like a set of elevator doors, two room doors, a door to the stairs, and then a door to the rooftop bar. And I really like this. I didn't think the in front of curtain moments really took away from last year's production, but I think adding this extra set piece has really helped them out. Just in terms of giving the audience an understanding of where our characters are in the hotel in which the majority of this show happens. I think it is good at like grounding us in "Oh, hey, this is where this is happening. This is where our other characters might be in relation to this moment, and this is where the characters on stage have just gone." So, we understand their kind of route through the hotel, shall we speak? Really enjoyed that. Beyond that, this isn't necessarily a change to the set itself, but a change to the venue that this show is taking place in. The Adelphi Theatre, which is the new home for this show for its limited run, is a very famous Art Deco Theatre, and I think this pairs beautifully with the 1961 setting that this play takes place in, because the play itself draws very heavily on Art Deco themes throughout both the edges of the proscenium arch that it is built in, as well as the set in the Piccadilly Hotel, too. So, I think it just feels so seamless when you are sat watching the show, still able to see elements of the Adelphi Theatre in your peripheral vision, but they blend so wonderfully with the show itself that it just it just makes sense. It's just chef's kiss, I love it. I also think the set is really cleverly designed because at no point does it feel like it distracts from what our performers are doing or overshadows them in any way. It is perfectly suited for the story that they are trying to tell and bringing the audience along, investing them not only in the Piccadilly Hotel as a setting, but also in the time period of that of the 1960s. This is aided, of course, by the costumes as well as the score. This 1961 setting is further solidified by the music that John Fibbit has put together. It's very jazzy, it's very brassy, it is very of the 1960s and I really really enjoy that. And it also evokes this very like James Bond-esque sound to it if you're familiar with like the iconic James Bond score at all. It works really well in making this feel like a spy thriller whilst at the same time the show is entirely like a complete farce of a slapstick goes wrong kind of spy mission, I suppose. Another thing along with the set that was slightly changed were a couple of jokes here and there. With the biggest one being the elevator shaft scene. Now, the elevator shaft scene is probably the one that I noticed was the most different. This time round, as Bernard is going down the elevator shaft, there are moments where there's like signs that are like, "Why are you doing this? This is a terrible idea. Turn back now, Bernard." and all of that, which was really really funny, not least because I didn't expect it. Of course, I was familiar with a lot of other jokes in the show, whereas this was a new one. So, caught me really by surprise the first time I went to see it. And then the other one is when Lance Buchanan falls down the elevator shaft. Previously, once he'd fallen down, the doors opened and it was Mr. Tipton in Australia being like, "Oh, you've fallen down to basically the Piccadilly Hotel Australia." Joke being he's fallen that far. This time, however, he falls down and then we get the lobby set reappear, and Janet Lance Piggott's mom pulls him out of the elevator shaft, which again, really entertaining joke. I think I preferred the Australia one, but understand why it was maybe replaced because this new joke does fit a lot better. I also think what's really lovely about the Comedy About Spies is that no matter how many times you see it, it's going to be a different show every time, be it because of the combination of cast members you have on stage, or the fact that one of them maybe gets the giggles, or they just decide to do something different in a different moment. For example, the last time I went to go and see it, instead of just taking Sergey's banana and squeezing it in her hand and dropping it on the floor as Elena, this time Bryony decided to take the banana and shove it in Chris Lees's mouth, and that nearly made him lose it. And I think it's moments like that that really endears you to a production like this. Though, of course, it is a moment you would only really get if you'd seen the show more than once. We also had Matt Cavendish on as Bananad, and he walked into like the laundry closet where Janet and Lance were waiting on him, and Nancy Zamit was playing Janet as he appeared through the door, accidentally spilt her drink down her blouse, which gave her the giggles, which then meant Matt didn't start the scene off correctly, so fully in character, he just goes, "Should I go out and come back in and do the scene properly?" Like, fully in character. And like I say, these are moments you'd only know were funny haha moments if you'd seen the show if you were lucky enough like me to see the show more than once. But, I do think it is such a big part of what makes Mischief shows so brilliant, they are different every time, even if they're following the same recipe each and every time. My biggest disappointment with the Comedy About Spies, to be honest, is the fact it's on such a limited run. I'd have this as a permanent fixture in the West End if I could. I love this show that much. And I do hope at the end of this run we have news as to what the future of this production is going to be, whether that's a UK tour or a transfer somewhere. I would love to know, cuz I do think this is one of Mischief's best productions by far to this day. So, if you haven't thought about it, I highly encourage you to go and check out the Comedy About Spies because I love it that much. It is a five-star show. I loved it back in 2025 and 2026 is no exception. But, those are all of my thoughts and feelings on the Comedy About Spies. So, if you've already seen it yourself, I'd love to know what you think about it. If you haven't seen it, go and see it and then come right back here to tell me what you thought about it. And, as always, if you want to stay up-to-date with the latest greatest theater news and reviews, then make sure you are following me so you never miss out.
